**Surat Ta-Ha**

On His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Ta-Ha﴾. There are seven opinions about it.

First: it is in Syriac, meaning "O man." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid. al-Tabari reported that it is in Nabataean, meaning "O man." Ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi said the same.

al-Kalbi said: it is the dialect of the tribe of ʿUkl. Qutrub said: it is in the dialect of the tribe of Tayyi'. He recited the verse of Yazid ibn Muhalhil:

*Indeed, foolishness (Ta-Ha) is among your characteristics;*
*may God not sanctify the souls of the accursed.*

[p. 393]

Second: it is one of the names of God, Exalted, and an oath that He swore by. This is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Third: it is the name of the surah and its key (opening).

Fourth: it is an abbreviation of a statement, whose knowledge God reserved for His Messenger.

Fifth: these are disjointed letters, each of which indicates a meaning.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verses 9–10:

(p. 395) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ That is, the account of Moses has reached you, concerning what his Lord chose him for prophethood and entrusted him with His message.

This may be by what He related to him in this place, and it may be by what He informed him of elsewhere.

﴿When he saw a fire﴾ It was fire to Moses, and light to God. Muqatil said: it was on a Friday night in winter.

﴿So he said to his family: "Wait here"﴾ That is, remain.

The difference between mukth (staying for a while) and iqamah (residing) is that iqamah lasts, while mukth does not last.

﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾ Concerning this there are two interpretations: First, "I saw a fire."

Second, "I felt companionship with a fire."

﴿Perhaps I will bring you from it a burning brand﴾ That is, a fire by which you may warm yourselves.

﴿Or find at the fire guidance﴾ Concerning this there are two interpretations: First, a guide who will show me the way, as said by Qatadah.

Second, a sign by which I may find the way.

They had lost their way, so they remained in their place after Moses left for three days, until a shepherd of the village passed by them and informed them of Moses' journey. So they returned with the shepherd to their village and stayed there for forty years until Moses accomplished the command of his Lord.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When he came to it﴾, meaning the fire, which was light. ﴿He was called: "O Moses! Indeed I am your Lord"﴾. Regarding this calling there are two views. The first: He alone addressed him with this calling.

The second: God made the light speak with this calling, so it was from His light, which was not separate from Him, and it became a calling from Him. His Lord informed him of it so that his soul would be at ease and would bear His command. He preceded his instruction with His saying: ﴿So take off your sandals﴾, and the verse continues.

Regarding the command to remove them, there are two views. The first: so that he would touch the blessed pool of the sacred valley with his feet. This was said by Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan, and Ibn Jurayj.

The second: because his sandals were made of the skin of a dead donkey. This was said by Ka'b, Ikrimah, and Qatadah.

﴿Indeed you are in the sacred valley﴾. On this there are two views. The first: "sacred" means "blessed." This was said by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

The second: it means "purified." This was said by Qutrub, and the poet said:

"You are one who joins the kinsfolk, a chief free from blemishes, a sacred benefactor."

On ﴿Tuwa﴾ there are five interpretations. The first: it is a name derived from "tawa" (folded), because he passed through its valley at night and it folded him up. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: it was named Tuwa because God called to him twice. In their speech, "tuwa" means "twice," because when a second thing follows the first, it becomes as though folded over it.

The third: rather, it was named so because the valley was sanctified twice. This was said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: the meaning of "tuwa" is: tread the valley with your foot. This was said by Mujahid.

The fifth: it is the name of the valley from of old. This was said by Ibn Zayd. So Moses removed his sandals and threw them behind the valley.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾. On this there are three interpretations. The first: establish prayer so that you remember Me in it. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: establish prayer with My remembrance, because one does not enter into prayer except by remembering Him.

The third: establish prayer whenever you remember it. This was said by Ibrahim.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it." Then God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾.

(p-399) ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ This is not a question seeking information; it is a question for confirmation, lest doubt enter upon him after it turned into a moving serpent.

﴿He said: It is my staff﴾. His answer thus contained two matters. The first: informing that it is a staff, and this answer is sufficient.

The second: attributing it to his possession. This is an addition he mentioned so that the answer would be more than what he was asked about.

Then he informed about its uses, though he had not been asked about them, to make clear his great need for it and his reliance on it, lest he appear indifferent to carrying it. So he said: ﴿I lean upon it, and I beat down [leaves] with it for my sheep﴾; that is, I strike the leaves off the trees with it so that my sheep may graze on them.

The rajiz (rhymed-verse reciter) said:

"I beat down with the staff for my flock the tender leaves of the arak and the basham."

ʿIkrima recited (wa-ahussu) with an unpointed sin.

Regarding al-hashsh and al-hass there are two views: First: they are two dialects with one meaning. Second: their meanings differ; al-hashsh with the pointed shin means striking the leaves from trees, and al-hass without pointing means driving the sheep.

﴿And for me in it are other uses﴾; that is, other needs. He specified the necessary use and alluded to the incidental ones. On this there are three views: First: he would drive wild beasts away with it, as Muqatil said. Second: he would strike fire with it and extract water with it. (p-400) Third: it would give light for him at night, as al-Dahhak said.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verses 22–35:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And draw your hand close to your side (lit. wing)﴾. There are three interpretations regarding it. The first: to your upper arm (ʿadud), as said by Mujahid.

The second: to your collar (jayb).

The third: to your side (janb), and He used "wing" to refer to the side, because the side is inclined at the place of the wing.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿My Lord, expand for me my breast﴾. It admits of two interpretations. The first: for the preservation of His private communication (with Him). The second: for conveying His message.

﴿And ease for me my task﴾. It admits of two interpretations. The first: [that He not burden me with] what I cannot bear. The second: [He grant me] help in carrying out what You have entrusted to me.

﴿And untie a knot from my tongue﴾. Regarding it there are three interpretations. The first: it was a knot in his tongue from the ember that he had put in his mouth in his childhood in the presence of Pharaoh.

The second: it was a knot in his tongue during his private communication with his Lord, so that he would not speak to anyone else except with His permission.

The third: his shyness before God from speaking to others after his private communication (with Him).

﴿That they may understand my speech﴾. It admits of two interpretations. The first: by the clarification of his speech. The second: by their affirming his words.

﴿And appoint for me a minister (wazir) from my family﴾. He asked God to appoint for him a minister, but he did not intend that (the role) be restricted to the ministry, so that he would be a partner in prophethood. Otherwise, it would have been permissible for him to appoint him as minister without asking.

﴿Aaron, my brother﴾. ﴿Strengthen through him my back (azr)﴾. Regarding it there are two interpretations. The first: that the azr is the back at the place of the two loins, and its meaning is: strengthen my self through him.

Abu Talib said:

*Did not our father Hashim strengthen his back (azrahu),
and enjoin his sons to thrust with spears and to strike?*

The second: that he be a helper through whom my affair is set right.

The poet said:

*I strengthened my back (azri) through him, and I was certain that he
is a brother in hardship, when one's ways are constricted for him.*

So the request in the first interpretation is for his own sake, and in the second it is for the sake of prophethood.

Aaron was three years older than Moses. On Aaron's forehead there was a mole (shāmah), and on Moses' nose there was a mole, and on the tip of his tongue [a mole].

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verses 36–40:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾. On this there are four opinions. The first: "I made you beloved to My servants." This was said by Salma ibn Kumayl.

The second: it means beauty and comeliness. This was said by Ikrimah.

The third: it means My mercy. This was said by Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari).

The fourth: "I made whoever saw you love you, until Pharaoh loved you, so you were spared his evil, and Asiya bint Muzahim loved you, so she adopted you." This was said by Ibn Zayd.

It may also bear a fifth meaning: that its meaning is, "I made My love for you manifest upon you, and this is a blessing upon you, because whomever Allah loves, He places His love in hearts."

﴿And that you might be reared under My eye﴾. On this there are two opinions. The first: "that you might be nourished according to My will." This was said by Qatadah.

The second: "that you might be raised under the eyes of your mother, with what she did with you of casting you into the river, while I was watching."

It may also bear a third meaning: "that you might be taken into care and raised according to My choice." The phrase ﴿under My eye﴾ may bear two meanings: the first, "according to My choice and My will"; the second, "by My protection and My care."

﴿So that her eye might be comforted and she would not grieve﴾. This may bear two meanings: the first, "her eye would be comforted by your safety and she would not grieve over your separation."

The second, "she would be comforted by your being taken into her care and would not grieve over your maintenance."

﴿And you killed a soul﴾, meaning the Copt.

﴿And We delivered you from distress﴾. This may bear two meanings: the first, "We saved you from retaliation (qawd)."

The second, "We granted you security from fear."

﴿And We tried you with a trying﴾. On this there are four sayings. The first: "We informed you until you became fit for prophethood."

The second: "We tested you with trial after trial." This was said by Qatadah.

The third: "We rescued you with a rescue from one ordeal after another. The first of them: his mother carried him in the year in which Pharaoh was slaughtering the male infants, then his being cast into the river; then his refusal of suckling except from his mother's breast; then his pulling at Pharaoh's beard until Pharaoh intended to kill him; then his grasping the ember instead of the date, whereby the killing of Pharaoh was averted from him; then the coming of a man from his own faction running to warn of what they had resolved upon regarding his killing." This was said by Ibn Abbas.

Mujahid said: "We purified you with purification."

﴿Then you came upon a decree, O Musa﴾. On this there are two opinions. The first: "upon a decree of the message and prophethood." This was said by Qatadah.

The second: "upon an appointed time." This was said by Qatadah and Mujahid.

It may also bear a third meaning: "you came upon a measure of hardship and an appointed term," and the poet said:

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verses 41–44:

﴿And I have chosen you for Myself﴾. Two meanings are possible. The first: "I created you," derived from ṣan'ah (craft, making). The second: "I chose you," derived from ṣanī'ah (favour, kindness).

"For Myself" has two meanings. The first: "for My love." The second: "for My message."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not slacken in remembering Me﴾. On this there are four opinions. The first: "Do not falter in remembering Me." The poet said:

"So Muhammad did not slacken, since God forgave him what had passed and what remained."

The second: "Do not weaken in My message." This was said by Qatadah.

The third: "Do not become lax (in calling to Me)." This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: "Do not cease." This was related by Aban, who cited the verse of Tarafah:

"As if the cauldrons set firm before them were domes whose builders never cease, always boiling."

(p-405) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So speak to him a gentle word﴾. On this there are two meanings. The first: "gentle and tender." The second: "address him by a kunyah (honorific name)," said by al-Suddi. It is said that Pharaoh's kunyah was Abu Murrah, and it is also said Abu al-Walid.

It may also bear a third meaning: to begin with hope before fear, so that he is softened by it and then prepared for fear, threat and warning. Some of the Sufis said: "O Lord, this is Your gentleness toward one who opposed You; how then is Your gentleness toward one who befriended You?" It is also said that Pharaoh had been good to Musa when he raised him, so he wished to make his gentleness toward him a repayment, since Musa could not repay him.

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿that he may hasten against us﴾ has two interpretations. The first: that he may hurry to act against us. The rajiz (the reciter of rajaz verse) said:

"The unbeliever (ʿilj) has hastened against us and rushed."

The second: that he may punish us with the punishment of one who has gone ahead (fāriṭ) in sin, that is, one who precedes in it. This was said by al-Mubarrad, and it is said that one who exceeds in a matter is called afraṭa (one who goes to excess), while one who falls short in it is called farraṭa (one who neglects).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verse 49–52:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation, then guided it﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations.

The first: He gave everything its mate from its own kind, then guided it to its mating. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Suddi.

The second: He gave everything its form, then guided it to its livelihood, its food and its drink. This was said by Mujahid. The poet said:

"For every thing He has a form (khilqa), and so God does whatever He wills."

By khilqa he means the form (ṣūra).

The third: He gave each thing what sustains it, then guided it to it. This was said by Qatadah.

It may also bear a fourth meaning: He gave everything the knowledge or craft He inspired in it, and guided it to knowing how to use it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So what is the state of the earlier generations?﴾ The word qurun is the plural of qarn, and a qarn is the people of each age; it is derived from their being "united" (qiranuhum) in it.

Al-Zajjaj said: the qarn is the people of each age, in which there is a prophet or a high rank in knowledge. He took it from the coupling (iqtiran) of the people of the age with the people of knowledge. So when there is a time in which there is a lull (fatra) and the dominance of ignorance, it is not a qarn.

Regarding Pharaoh's question about the generations, there are four views:

The first: he asked about them in relation to what Moses called him to of faith, namely whether they were upon the same as what he calls to or contrary to it.

The second: he said this to him as a way of cutting off the call and warding off an answer.

The third: he asked about their sin and their recompense.

The fourth: when he called him to acknowledge the resurrection, he said: "What is the state of the earlier generations, that they were not resurrected?" ﴿He said: Their knowledge is with my Lord﴾, so Moses referred the knowledge of that to his Lord.

﴿In a Book﴾ ﴿My Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾, meaning He did not place the knowledge of that in a Book because He errs or forgets.

The placing of it in the Book may bear two meanings: the first is that it is a favour from Him to Himself and a judgment by Him; the second is that He makes His angels aware of it at its appointed time.

Regarding His saying ﴿My Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾ there are two views: the first is that He makes no mistake concerning it and does not leave it out. The second is that the Book does not go astray from my Lord, nor does my Lord forget what is in the Book. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Muqatil said: At that [time] Moses did not have knowledge of the earlier generations, because he had learned it from the Torah, and it was not revealed to him until after the destruction and drowning of Pharaoh.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verses 57–59:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿a place equitable﴾ (makanan suwa). On this there are four interpretations:

First: fair between them (munsifan baynahum).

Second: a just arrangement between us and you, said by Qatadah and al-Suddi.

Third: a just and middle place (adlan wasatan), said by Abu Ubayda, who recited:

"Indeed our father had settled in a land, suwa between Qays, Qays of Aylan, and al-Ghazar."

Fourth: an even, level place in which what we have made clear will become evident to the people, said by Ibn Zayd.

(p-409) It is also read as suwa with a damma on the sin and with a kasra. On both readings there are two views: first, that their meanings are the same even though their wording differs; second, that their meanings differ, so that with the damma it means "impartial" (al-munsif), and with the kasra it means "just" (al-adl).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿the Day of Adornment﴾ (yawm al-zinah). On this there are four sayings:

First: that it was a festival day for them, said by Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Ishaq.

Second: the day of Saturday (yawm al-sabt), said by al-Dahhak.

Third: Ashura, said by Ibn Abbas.

Fourth: that it was a market day on which they would adorn themselves, said by Qatadah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verse 60–64:

Allah's words: ﴿Do not fabricate against Allah a lie﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: do not fabricate against Allah a lie through your sorcery.

The second: through denying me and saying that what I have brought is sorcery.

﴿Lest He destroy you with a punishment﴾: that is, lest He ruin you and uproot you. al-Farazdaq said:

"And time has bitten, O son of Marwan, leaving of wealth nothing but what is stripped bare (musahhat) or ruined (mujallaf)."

So the musahhat is the one that has been uprooted, and the mujallaf is the one that has been destroyed.

﴿Then they disputed among themselves their affair﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: concerning the ropes and staves they had prepared; this was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: concerning who would be the first to cast.

﴿And they concealed their private counsel﴾. Concerning this there are four sayings.

The first: the private counsel they concealed was that they said: "If this is sorcery, we will overcome it; and if it is from the sky, then its command belongs to Him." This was said by Qatadah.

The second: that when he said to them ﴿Woe to you﴾ and the rest of the verse, they said: "This is not the speech of a sorcerer." This was said by Ibn Munabbih.

The third: that they concealed their counsel from Musa and Harun, by their saying ﴿Indeed, these two are certainly sorcerers﴾ and the verses that follow. This was said by Muqatil and al-Suddi.

The fourth: that they concealed their counsel: "If Musa overcomes us, we will follow him." This was said by al-Kalbi.

Allah's words: ﴿They said: Indeed these two are certainly sorcerers﴾. This is the reading of Abu 'Amr, and it agrees with the grammar (i'rab) but disagrees with the Mushaf (the codified written text of the Qur'an).

Most readers recited: "inna hadhani al-sahiran" (إنْ هَذانِ السّاحِرانِ), and in this they agreed with the Mushaf. Then they differed over the shaddah (emphasis) on inna. Ibn Kathir and Hafs lightened it (inna), and both were saved by lightening inna from disagreeing with the Mushaf and from corrupting the grammar; its meaning is: "These two are none but sorcerers."

Ubayy recited: "inna dhani illa sahiran" (إنَّ ذانِ إلّا ساحِرانِ). The rest of the readers recited with the shaddah: "inna hadhani la-sahiran" (إنَّ هَذانَ لَساحِرانِ).

They agreed with the Mushaf but opposed the apparent grammar.

Those who read thus differed about its grammatical analysis according to four sayings:

The first: this is according to the dialect of Bilharith ibn Ka'b and Kinanah ibn Zayd, who make the nominative, accusative and genitive of the dual with the alif. They recite:

"So he lowered his head like a brave man's lowering, and had he seen an opening, his two fangs would have been sharp" (fa-atraqa itraqa al-shuja'...).

The second aspect: the Qur'an may not be carried over to what is deviant among dialects and turned away from its most eloquent and sound form. Rather, in inna there is a hidden ha' (pronoun), its estimate being: "innahu hadhani la-sahiran," and this is the saying of the earlier grammarians.

The third: he built hadhani on a form that does not change in grammatical case, just as he built alladhina on this pattern for the accusative and nominative.

The fourth: the emphatic inna in this place means "yes," as a man said to Ibn al-Zubayr: "May Allah curse the she-camel that carried me to you," and Ibn al-Zubayr said: "Inna, and her companion."

Abdullah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat said:

"The blamers wept over my youthful passion, and they blame me and I blame them. And they say, 'Gray hair has risen upon you, and you have grown old,' so I said, 'Inna'" (that is, "yes").

﴿And they would take away your ideal way of life﴾: concerning the speaker of this there are three sayings. The first: it is the speech of the sorcerers. The second: it is the speech of Pharaoh's people. The third: it is the speech of Pharaoh alone among his people, though it may be indicated to refer to their group.

Concerning its interpretation there are five aspects. The first: "and they would take away the people of intellect and nobility." This was said by Mujahid.

The second: "with the Children of Israel, who were of number and wealth." This was said by Qatadah.

The third: "and they would take away with the way of life you are upon in conduct." This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: "and they would take away your religion and your worship of Pharaoh." This was said by al-Dahhak.

The fifth: "and they would take away the people of your ideal way," [and al-muthla is the feminine of al-amthal], and what is meant by al-amthal is the most excellent. Abu Talib said:

"And by the life of Allah, if indeed what I see is real, our swords will surely mingle with the most excellent."

Allah's words: ﴿Then gather your plan﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: gather your group upon their affair in the plotting against Musa and Harun.

The second: its meaning is: firm up your affair. The rajiz said:

"Would that I knew, though wishes do not benefit, whether I will go one day while my affair is gathered (mujma')."

That is, firm (muhkam).

﴿Then come in ranks (saffan)﴾: that is, line up and do not mix.

﴿He who prevails (istala)﴾: that is, he who overcomes.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "No, rather you throw"﴾ to the end of the verse.

Regarding Musa's command to the sorcerers to cast (their staffs), although that would be disbelief which it is not permissible for him to command, there are two explanations. The first: the wording takes the form of a command, but its meaning is that of a statement, and its implied sense is: "If your casting is a proof in your view, then cast."

The second: that command came from him as a demonstration (i'tibar, a lesson or display) so that he could show them the validity of his prophethood and the clarity of his proof, and that what nullified the sorcery was not itself sorcery.

They differed about the number of the sorcerers. It is related from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah that they were seventy thousand sorcerers. It is related from Ibn Jurayj that they were nine hundred sorcerers: three hundred from al-Arish, three hundred from al-Fayyum, and they were uncertain about the three hundred from Alexandria. Abu Salih related from Ibn Abbas that they were seventy-two sorcerers, of whom two were Copts and seventy were from the Children of Israel. They were sorcerers at the beginning of the day and martyrs at its end.

﴿It appeared to him, because of their sorcery, that their staffs and ropes were moving﴾ has two possible meanings. The first: that this appearance was to Pharaoh. The second: that it was to Musa in the same way.

﴿So Musa sensed fear within himself﴾: regarding this fear there are two explanations. The first: he feared that the people's affair would become confused, so that they would suppose the sorcerers had done the same as his deed and that it was of the same kind. The second: it was the caution (hadhar) inherent in human nature.

"Awjasa" means "concealed" (asarra).

﴿We said, "Do not fear"﴾ to the end of the verse: to steady him and to remove his fear.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow what they have made﴾. That is, it will seize it in its mouth and swallow it quickly. It is said that it swallowed the load of three hundred camels of ropes and staffs. Then Musa took it, and it returned to being a staff as it had been.

Regarding the staff there are two statements. The first: it was made of wild jujube (awsaj), related by Wahb. The second: it was from Paradise, related by Ibn Abbas, who said: "With it Musa killed Uj ibn Anaq."

﴿So the sorcerers were thrown down prostrate﴾: in obedience to Allah and in confirmation of Musa.

﴿They said, "We believe in the Lord of Harun and Musa"﴾: that is, in the Lord to whom Harun and Musa called, because He is a Lord to us and to all creation. It is said that they did not raise their heads until they saw Paradise and the reward of its people, and at that moment...

Abu Salih related from Ibn Abbas that they were seventy-two sorcerers, of whom two were Copts and seventy were from the Children of Israel. They were sorcerers at the beginning of the day and martyrs at its end.

﴿It appeared to him, because of their sorcery, that their staffs and ropes were moving﴾ has two possible meanings. The first: that this appearance was to Pharaoh. The second: that it was to Musa in the same way.

﴿So Musa sensed fear within himself﴾: regarding this fear there are two explanations. The first: he feared that the people's affair would become confused, so that they would suppose the sorcerers had done the same as his deed and that it was of the same kind. The second: it was the caution (hadhar) inherent in human nature.

"Awjasa" means "concealed" (asarra).

﴿We said, "Do not fear"﴾ to the end of the verse: to steady him and to remove his fear.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow what they have made﴾. That is, it will seize it in its mouth and swallow it quickly. It is said that it swallowed the load of three hundred camels of ropes and staffs. Then Musa took it, and it returned to being a staff as it had been.

Regarding the staff there are two statements. The first: it was made of wild jujube (awsaj), related by Wahb. The second: it was from Paradise, related by Ibn Abbas, who said: "With it Musa killed Uj ibn Anaq."

﴿So the sorcerers were thrown down prostrate﴾: in obedience to Allah and in confirmation of Musa.

﴿They said, "We believe in the Lord of Harun and Musa"﴾: that is, in the Lord to whom Harun and Musa called, because He is a Lord to us and to all creation. It is said that they did not raise their heads until they saw Paradise and the reward of its people, and at that moment...

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 20, verses 71–73:**

﴿They said, "We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us"﴾. It is said that the wife of Pharaoh used to ask, "Who has prevailed?" It was told to her, "Musa and Harun."

She said, "I believe in the Lord of Musa and Harun." Pharaoh sent for her and said, "Take the largest rock and threaten her with it. If she persists in her statement, [then throw it upon her]." [God] took her soul, and the rock was dropped upon her body, and there was no spirit in it.

﴿And by He who created us﴾: there are two views concerning this. The first is that it is an oath.

The second is that it means [no] "by He who created us."

﴿So decide what you are going to decide﴾: there are two views concerning this.

(p-415) The first is: "Do what you are going to do."

The second is: "Judge as you are going to judge."

﴿You only decide concerning this worldly life﴾: this may have two meanings. The first is: your authority and your punishment are only in this worldly life, not in the Hereafter.

The second is: what passes away and goes is this worldly life, while the Hereafter remains.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God is better and more enduring﴾: there are two views concerning this. The first is: God is better than you and more enduring in reward if He is obeyed, and in punishment if He is disobeyed.

The second is: He is better than you in reward if He is obeyed, and more enduring than you in punishment if He is disobeyed.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verses 74–76:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿He will neither die therein nor live﴾ admits of two interpretations. The first: he does not benefit from his life, nor does he find rest in his death, as the poet said:

؎ Ala man li-nafsin la tamutu fa-yanqadi shaqaha wa la tahya hayatan laha ta'mu

(Is there anyone who can help a soul that does not die, so that its misery might end, and that does not live a life that has any sweetness?)

The second: the soul of the disbeliever is suspended at his throat, as God has informed about him, so he does not die by its departure, ﴿nor live by its settling﴾.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verse 77–79:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You shall not fear being overtaken, nor shall you be afraid.﴾ Ibn Jurayj said: The companions of Musa said to him: "This is Pharaoh, who has overtaken us, and this is the sea, which has encompassed us," so Allah revealed this verse.

That is: you shall not fear being overtaken by Pharaoh, nor shall you be afraid of drowning in the sea if it surrounds you.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verse 80–82:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not transgress therein﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: do not disbelieve in it (ka-farū bihi).

The second: do not store any of it for more than a day and a night. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "So it bred worms over them, what they had stored. Had it not been for that, food would never have bred worms."

The third: do not seek help with My provision in disobeying Me.

﴿Lest My wrath descend upon you﴾. It has been recited with a ḍammah on the ḥāʾ and with a kasrah. Its meaning with the ḍammah is "descends" (yunzilu), and with the kasrah is "becomes binding" (yajibu).

﴿Then he has certainly fallen﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. One: he has fallen into the Fire.

The second: he has perished in this world.

His saying, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And indeed, I am Forgiving toward whoever repents, believes, and does righteous work﴾. That is, Forgiving toward whoever repents from polytheism. ﴿And believes﴾, meaning in Allah and His Messenger. And does righteous work, meaning acting upon His commands and stopping at His prohibitions.

﴿Then remains guided﴾. Concerning this there are six interpretations. The first: then he did not doubt his faith. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: he held fast to faith until he dies. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: then he adhered to the sunnah of His Prophet (ﷺ). This was said by al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas.

The fourth: then he attained (correct) action. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: then he recognized the recompense of his deed, of good with reward or of evil with punishment. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The sixth: then he was guided regarding the guardianship of the People of the House of the Prophet (ﷺ). This was said by Thabit.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verse 83–89:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿angry, grieving﴾ (ghadban asifan). Regarding it there are five interpretations. The first: asaf (grief) is the intensest form of anger.

The second: it means sorrowful; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, and al-Suddi.

The third: it means distressed (jazaʿ); this was said by Mujahid.

The fourth: it means one who regrets (mutanaddim).

The fifth: it means one who is filled with sorrow over what has passed (mutahassir).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Did your Lord not promise you a good promise?﴾ Regarding it there are four opinions. The first: that He promised them victory and triumph.

The second: that it is His saying: ﴿And indeed I am Most Forgiving﴾ (Qur'an 20:82), and so on.

(p-418) The third: the Torah, in which there is guidance and light, so that they might act in accordance with what is in it and thereby merit the reward of their deeds.

The fourth: that it is what He promised them in the Hereafter in return for holding fast to His religion in this world; this was said by al-Hasan.

And regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So you broke your appointment with me﴾ (fa-akhlaftum mawidi), there are two aspects. One of them: that He promised them, right after that, an appointment for the meeting (al-miqat), but they delayed.

﴿They said: We did not break our appointment with you by our own will﴾ (bi-maliknā). Regarding it there are three interpretations. The first: by our own power (bi-taqatina); this was said by Qatadah and al-Suddi.

The second: we did not have control over ourselves at that time because of the calamity that befell us; this was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: the believers did not have the power to prevent the foolish ones from that, and the appointment they broke was that He promised them forty [days], and they counted the forty as twenty days and twenty nights, and they thought that they had completed the appointed term. And al-Samiri assured them that they had completed it.

﴿But we were laden with burdens of the people's adornments﴾. That is, we were laden with the ornaments of the people of Pharaoh; because Musa had commanded them to borrow from their ornaments; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and al-Suddi.

It was also said: they were made into a load (hamlan).

And al-Awzar (burdens) means loads. This may be understood in two ways. One: that it means the burdens of sins, because there had been embezzlement (ghulul) among them.

The second: that it means the weight of the load, because it weighed them down and weighed down their feet.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Thus al-Samiri cast [it]﴾, the verse.

Qatadah said: when the people were slow in returning, and Musa was delayed, al-Samiri said to them: he has only been delayed on your account, because of the ornaments that you have. So they gathered them and handed them over to al-Samiri, and he fashioned from them a calf. Then he cast upon it a handful he had taken from the trace of the Messenger, who was Jibril. Mamar said: the horse upon which Jibril was mounted was the life-giving steed; so when he cast the handful upon it, it became a calf with a body that had a lowing sound (khuwar).

(p-419) Al-Khuwar is the sound of a bull, and regarding it there are two opinions. One: that it was a sound of life which He created, because the molten calf was transformed by the handful from the trace of the Messenger, and it became a living animal; this was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Suddi. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the calf lowed one single lowing and did not follow it with another like it.

The second: that its lowing and its sound were by means of the wind, because he made holes in it, and when the wind entered it, it lowed, and there was no life in it; this was said by Mujahid.

﴿So they said: This is your god and the god of Musa﴾. That is, al-Samiri said to the people of Musa after he had finished with the calf: this is your god and the god of Musa, meaning so that they would hasten to worship it.

﴿But he forgot﴾ (fa-nasiya). Regarding it there are four opinions. The first: al-Samiri forgot his Islam and his faith; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: al-Samiri forgot what he had said to them: "Musa has forgotten his god with you"; this was said by Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

The third: he forgot that his people would not believe him in worshipping a calf that neither harms nor benefits; this was said by Ibn Bahr.

The fourth: that Musa forgot that his people had worshipped the calf after him; this was said by Mujahid.

﴿Do they not see that it does not return to them a word﴾. That is, do the Children of Israel not see that the calf they worshipped does not return to them any answer?

﴿And it does not possess for them any harm or benefit﴾? How then could it be a god?

Muqatil said: when five and thirty days had passed of the appointment of Musa, al-Samiri commanded the Children of Israel to gather what they had borrowed of the ornaments of the people of Pharaoh, and he fashioned it into a calf on the sixth, the thirty-seventh, and the thirty-eighth [days]; and he called them to worship the calf on the ninth; and they responded to him. And Musa came to them after the completion of the forty [days].

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verse 90–94:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray?"﴾ He means by worshipping the calf.

﴿That you did not follow me﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions. One: that you did not follow me in going out, and you did not stand with those who had gone astray.

The second: that you did not follow my practice in preventing them and denouncing them. This was said by Muqatil.

﴿Did you then disobey my command?﴾ ﴿And Musa said to his brother Harun, "Take my place among my people, act righteously, and do not follow the way of the corrupters."﴾ When he remained with them and did not exert himself in preventing them and denouncing them, he attributed to him disobedience and opposition to his command.

﴿He said, "O son of my mother"﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions. One: because he was his brother of both father and mother.

The second: that he was his brother of the father only, not of the mother. He said "O son of my mother" only to soften him and to win his compassion.

﴿Do not seize my beard nor my head﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions. One: that he seized his hair with his right hand and his beard with his left, as said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that he seized his ear and his beard, and he referred to the ear by "the head," which is the view of those who consider the ear part of the head.

There is a difference of opinion concerning the reason for his seizing his beard and head, on three views:

(p-421) The first: so that he could confide to him the descent of the Tablets upon him, because they had been revealed to him in this private conversation (munajat). He wanted to conceal them from the Children of Israel before repentance. So Harun said to him, "Do not seize my beard nor my head," so that his secret confidence would not appear to the Children of Israel.

The second: he did this because it occurred to his mind that Harun inclined toward the Children of Israel in what they had done regarding the calf, and such a thing is not permissible for the prophets.

The third, which is the most likely: he did this because Harun had refrained from denouncing the Children of Israel who worshipped the calf, and because of his remaining among them in their sins.

﴿Indeed I feared that you would say, "You have caused a division among the Children of Israel."﴾ This is Harun's answer to the words: ﴿Did you then disobey my command?﴾ Regarding it there are two opinions. One: you caused division among them through the difference that arose in their beliefs.

The second: you caused division among them by fighting those among them who worshipped the calf.

It was also said: they all worshipped it except twelve thousand who remained with Harun and did not worship it.

﴿And you did not observe my word﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions. One: you did not act upon my instruction, as said by Muqatil.

The second: you did not await my covenant, as said by Abu 'Ubaydah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verses 95–101:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿He said, "What is your matter, O Samiri?"﴾ Al-khatb (the matter, affair) is what occurs of great affairs for which one is addressed. The poet said:

(p-422)(

"My neighbour announced the imminent approach of departure, a virgin who openly declared a great affair."

Regarding the Samiri there are two opinions. The first is that he was a man from the people of Kirman who followed Musa from the Children of Israel; this was said by al-Tabari, and his name was Musa ibn Zafar.

Regarding his being called al-Samiri there are two opinions. The first: he was from a tribe called Samirah; this was said by Qatadah.

The second: because he was from a village called Samirah.

﴿He said, "I perceived what they did not perceive"﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: "I looked at what they did not look at"; this was said by Abu 'Ubaydah.

The second: "with what they did not discern"; this was said by Muqatil.

Regarding basura (بصرت) and absara (أبصرت) there are two views. The first: their meaning is one and the same. The second: their meanings differ, so absara means "I looked (nazartu)" and basura means "I understood (fatintu)."

﴿So I grasped a handful﴾. The majority read it with the emphatic dad (ض, qabdah), while al-Hasan read it with an unpointed sad (ص, qabsah). The difference between them is that qabdah with the dad is with the whole palm, and with the unpointed sad it is with the fingertips. ﴿from the footprint of the Messenger﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: the Messenger is Jibril.

(p-423) Regarding how he recognised him there are two opinions. The first: because he had seen him on the day the sea was split, so he recognised him.

The second: when his mother bore him, she placed him in a cave out of fear for him from Pharaoh, who was killing the Children of Israel; Jibril was nourishing him as a child for the sake of the trial, so he recognised him when he grew up. He took a handful of dust from the hoofprint of his horse and tied it in his garment. ﴿Then I threw it﴾, meaning I cast it. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: he cast it into what he had melted of the ornaments in forming the calf, so that it lowed after its forming.

The second: he cast it into the inside of the calf after its forming, so that its lowing appeared. This is its explanation according to the view of those who take the Messenger to be Jibril.

The second opinion: the Messenger is Musa, and his footprint is his law which he instituted and his sunnah which he established. His saying, "So I grasped a handful from the footprint of the Messenger and threw it," means: I cast aside the law of Musa and discarded his sunnah, then I took the calf as a body that has a lowing.

﴿And thus my soul enticed me﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: "my soul spoke to me"; this was said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: "my soul adorned it for me"; this was said by al-Akhfash.

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿He said, "Go, for it is yours in this life to say, 'No touching.'"﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: his saying, "Go," was a threat from Musa, and therefore the Samiri became afraid and fled, wandering in the wilderness with the wild beasts and predators, finding no one among the people who would touch him, until he became like one who says "No touching," due to his distance from the people and their distance from him.

The poetess said:

"Bearer of banners with which there was a spear-bearer, until the Azd would say 'No touching.'"

(p-424) The second opinion: this statement from Musa was a prohibition upon the Samiri, and Musa commanded the Children of Israel not to eat with him nor mix with him, so he neither touched nor was touched. The poet said:

"Tamim are like the people of the Samiri and his saying: Surely the Samiri does not desire 'No touching.'"

That is, they do not associate with him and he is not associated with.

﴿And indeed, for you there is an appointment which you will not be able to break﴾. It may bear two meanings. The first: concerning respite, it will not be advanced. The second: concerning punishment, it will not be delayed.

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿His knowledge encompasses all things﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: He has encompassed everything, such that nothing has gone outside His knowledge. The second: His knowledge encompasses all things, such that nothing is void of His knowledge of it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verse 102–104:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And We shall gather the criminals that Day, blue-eyed﴾. Regarding this there are six opinions. The first: blind. This was said by al-Farra' (al-Farra', the grammarian).

The second: thirsty, their eyes having turned blue from the intensity of thirst. This was said by al-Azhari (al-Azhari, the lexicographer).

The third: the disfiguring of their creation, through the blueness of their eyes and the blackness of their faces.

The fourth: that it is false hope, since it is followed by disappointment, and this is a kind of punishment.

The fifth: that what is meant by blueness is the fixed staring of the eye from the intensity of fear. The poet said:

Your eyes have turned blue, O son of Mukaʿbar, as every Dabbi (Dabbi, a member of the tribe of Dabba) turns blue from baseness.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿They will whisper among themselves﴾, that is, they will speak secretly among themselves, from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not recite your prayer aloud or silently﴾ [al-Isra': 110], that is, do not recite it secretly.

﴿You remained not but ten [days]﴾. "Ten" is used in the sense of minimizing, not as a precise limit. Regarding this there are two views. The first: you remained in the world only ten [days], because of what they witnessed of the swiftness of the Resurrection. This was said by al-Hasan (al-Hasan al-Basri).

The second: you remained in your graves only ten [days], because of what matched it of the swiftness of recompense.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We know best what they say﴾. This admits of two meanings. The first: We know best what they say, of what they whisper among themselves.

The second: We know best what passes between them of speech concerning the durations they remained.

﴿When their best in conduct says﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: the most sound in intellect.

The second: the most correct in judgment.

﴿You remained not but a day﴾, because in his view it was the shorter period of time and the lesser stay. Then regarding this there are two views. The first: their stay in the world. The second: their stay in the graves.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verses 105–108:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿They will ask you about the mountains. Say: My Lord will blow them away with a blast﴾. On this there are two opinions. The first: He will make them like sand, then send the winds upon them, and they will scatter them as grain is winnowed.

(p-426) The second: they will become like scattered dust (al-haba').

﴿And leave it as a level plain﴾. Regarding al-qa' (the level ground) there are three sayings. The first: it is the even place in which there is no vegetation; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd. The second: the smooth earth. The third: a pool of standing water; this was said by al-Farra'.

Regarding al-saftsaf (the level plain) there are two views. The first: it is that in which there is no vegetation; this was said by al-Kalbi. The second: it is the even place, as if he said, in one straight row in its evenness; this was said by Mujahid.

﴿You will not see in it any crookedness or any elevation﴾. On this there are five sayings. The first: "crookedness" means a valley, and "elevation" (amt) means a hillock; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: "crookedness" means a crack, and "amt" means a mound; this was said by al-Hasan. The third: "crookedness" means a slope; and "amt" means a trace; this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. The fourth: al-amt is pulling and bending, and from it is the saying of the poet:

Verse: "There is no free movement of his stride from amt."

This was said by Qatadah. The fifth: al-amt is that a place in the open plain or the mountain becomes thick, and is thin in another place; this is related by al-Suli, so al-amt is from ascent and rising.

His exalted saying: ﴿And voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful, so you will not hear except a whisper﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, they will be humbled into silence. The poet said:(p-427)

Verse: "When the news of al-Zubayr came, the towers of Madinah and the humbled mountains split apart."

﴿except a whisper (hamsan)﴾. On this there are three sayings. The first: it is a faint sound; this was said by Mujahid. Verse: "And they walk with us in a whisper (hamisa)."

He means the sounds of the camels' soft feet in their march.

The second: "crookedness" means a crack, and "amt" means a mound; this was said by al-Hasan. The third: "crookedness" means a slope; and "amt" means a trace; this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. The fourth: al-amt is pulling and bending, and from it is the saying of the poet:

89 (

Verse: "There is no free movement of his stride from amt."

This was said by Qatadah. The fifth: al-amt is that a place in the open plain or the mountain becomes thick, and is thin in another place; this is related by al-Suli, so al-amt is from ascent and rising.

His exalted saying: ﴿And voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful, so you will not hear except a whisper﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, they will be humbled into silence. The poet said:(p-427)

Verse: "When the news of al-Zubayr came, the towers of Madinah and the humbled mountains split apart."

﴿except a whisper (hamsan)﴾. On this there are three sayings. The first: it is a faint sound; this was said by Mujahid. The second: the movement of the lips and tongue; Ubayy recited: "they will not speak except in a whisper." The third: the moving of feet; this was said by Ibn Zayd, and the reciter (al-rajiz) said:

Verse: "And they walk with us in a whisper (hamisa)."

He means the sounds of the camels' soft feet in their march.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verses 109–112:

His statement, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾. Concerning this there are five interpretations. The first: that is, they were humiliated (dhallat). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they were submissive (khashaʿat). This was said by Mujahid. The difference between humiliation (dhull) and submissiveness (khushuʿ), although their meanings are close, is that dhull means being humble in one's self, while khushuʿ means being lowly before one who is owed obedience.

Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"My face bowed to Him, and all my creation,
among those who prostrate to His face, is thankful."

The third: they acted (ʿamilat). This was said by al-Kalbi.

The fourth: they submitted (istaslamat). This was said by ʿAtiyyah al-ʿAwfi.

The fifth: it is the placing of the forehead and nose upon the ground in prostration. This was said by Talq ibn Habib.

Concerning ﴿al-Qayyum﴾ there are three interpretations. The first: that He is the one who stands over every soul with what it has earned. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: the one who stands in charge of the management of creation.

The third: the Everlasting, who does not cease or perish.

﴿And he has failed who carries injustice﴾: meaning shirk (associating partners with God).

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿So he will not fear injustice or diminution﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: he will not fear injustice by having his misdeeds increased, nor diminution by having his good deeds reduced. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second: he will not fear injustice by being left unrewarded for his deeds, nor diminution by having something of his due taken away. This was said by Ibn Zayd. The difference between injustice (zulm) and diminution (hadm) is that zulm is the withholding of the whole of a right, while hadm is the withholding of part of it. Diminution is a form of injustice, although they differ in one respect. Al-Mutawakkil al-Laythi said:

"Indeed, the humiliated and the base are a group
whose protector is the one who is diminished and wronged."

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah Ta-Ha, verses 113–114:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿or it brings them a reminder﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: caution (ḥadhar), said by Qatadah. The second: honour for their faith, said by al-Ḍaḥḥak. The third: a reminder by which they take warning.

(p. 429) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾, to the end of the verse.

Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: do not ask for its revelation before it is decreed, meaning before its revelation (waḥy) comes to you. The second: do not convey it to the people before the explanation of its interpretation (ta'wīl) comes to you, said by ʿAṭiyyah. The third: do not hasten in reciting it before Jibril has finished conveying it, because he used to hasten in reciting it before Jibril had finished conveying it, fearing that he would forget it, said by al-Kalbi.

﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾. This may bear four meanings. The first: increase me in adab (good conduct) in your religion, because what he needs of the knowledge of his religion, for himself or for his community, is not something God may delay for him until he seeks it from Him. The second: increase me in patience in Your obedience and in striving against Your enemies, because patience becomes easier with the presence of knowledge. The third: increase me in knowledge of the stories of Your prophets and the stations of Your awliyāʾ (friends). The fourth: increase me in knowledge of the state of my community and what it will be upon after me.

I found an answer attributed to al-Kalbi.

The fifth: its meaning is ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾, because whenever more of the Qur'an was revealed to him, he increased in knowledge of it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verses 115–122:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We had certainly taken a covenant from Adam﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: it means he abandoned the command of his Lord; this is what Mujahid said.

The second: that he forgot (nasiya), from forgetfulness (nisyan) and inattentiveness (sahw). Ibn 'Abbas said: "Man was only named insan (human) because he was given a covenant (uhida ilayhi) and then forgot (fa-nasiya)."

﴿And We did not find in him resolve (azm)﴾. Concerning this there are four interpretations. The first: patience (sabr); this is what Qatadah said.

The second: memorization (hifz); this is what 'Atiyyah said.

The third: steadfastness (thabat).

Ibn Umamah said: "If the deeds of the children of Adam were weighed against the forbearance (hilm) of Adam, his forbearance would outweigh theirs." And Allah has said: ﴿And We did not find in him resolve﴾.

The fourth: resolve in returning to the sin a second time.

His saying, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So let him not expel you both from the Garden, so that you would be distressed﴾. It means you and your wife, because the cause (illah) is equal in both of you.

He did not say "so that you both would be distressed" (fa-tashqa) for two reasons. The first: because he is the one addressed, not her. The second: because he is the one who toils and earns for her, so distress (shaqa) applies to him more specifically.

"The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever follows My guidance﴾ and acts upon what is in it, ﴿he will not go astray, nor will he suffer﴾ — he will not go astray in this world, nor will he suffer."

(p-431) Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah guaranteed for whoever recites the Qur'an and acts upon what is in it that he will not go astray in this world, nor will he suffer in the Hereafter.

﴿But whoever turns away from My remembrance — indeed, for him is a constricted life﴾. Concerning this there are four interpretations:

First: It is unlawful earnings. This was said by 'Ikrimah.

Second: His life will be troubled, in that he spends without believing in being replaced. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: It is the punishment of the grave. This was said by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu Hurayrah traced it back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Fourth: It is the food of ad-Dari' (thorny plant) and az-Zaqqum in Hell. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd.

Ad-Dank (ضَنْك), in their speech, means narrowness. 'Antarah said:

"Indeed, if death were to be given a form, it would take my form, when they alight in a constricted place."

It may also carry a fifth meaning: that he earns less than what suffices him.

﴿And We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations:

First: Blind in one state, and seeing in another state.

Second: Blind to the proof. This was said by Mujahid.

Third: Blind to the directions of goodness, not guided to any of them.

"The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever follows My guidance﴾ and acts upon what is in it, ﴿he will not go astray, nor will he suffer﴾ — he will not go astray in this world, nor will he suffer."

(p-431) Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah guaranteed for whoever recites the Qur'an and acts upon what is in it that he will not go astray in this world, nor will he suffer in the Hereafter.

﴿But whoever turns away from My remembrance — indeed, for him is a constricted life﴾. Concerning this there are four interpretations:

First: It is unlawful earnings. This was said by 'Ikrimah.

Second: His life will be troubled, in that he spends without believing in being replaced. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: It is the punishment of the grave. This was said by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu Hurayrah traced it back to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Fourth: It is the food of ad-Dari' (thorny plant) and az-Zaqqum in Hell. This was said by al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd.

Ad-Dank (ضَنْك), in their speech, means narrowness. 'Antarah said:

"Indeed, if death were to be given a form, it would take my form, when they alight in a constricted place."

It may also carry a fifth meaning: that he earns less than what suffices him.

﴿And We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations:

First: Blind in one state, and seeing in another state.

Second: Blind to the proof. This was said by Mujahid.

Third: Blind to the directions of goodness, not guided to any of them.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verses 127–130:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾, has two interpretations. The first: that He made the recompense the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: [it refers to] their being delayed until the Day of Badr.

﴿It would have been inevitable﴾ has two interpretations. The first: it would have been a binding punishment.

The second: it would have been a decree (qada'), said by al-Akhfash.

﴿And a specified term﴾ has two interpretations. The first: the Day of Badr.

The second: the Day of Resurrection, said by Qatadah.

He said: in the speech there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), and its meaning is: "Had it not been for a word and a specified term, it would have been inevitable."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾, meaning: over the harm and the slander.

﴿And glorify your Lord with His praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting﴾. Before the rising of the sun is the Fajr prayer, and before its setting is the 'Asr prayer.

﴿And during the hours of the night﴾: its hours, singular inan (ínan), and in it there are two interpretations. The first: it is the prayer of the whole night, said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is the Maghrib and the late 'Isha' prayers.

﴿And at the ends of the day﴾, in which there are two interpretations. The first: the Fajr prayer, because it is the end of the first half and the beginning of the second half, said by Qatadah.

The second: that it is the voluntary prayer, said by al-Hasan.

(p-433) ﴿So that you may be well-pleased﴾, i.e., that you may be given. 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read ﴿turdha﴾ with a dammah on the ta', meaning: perhaps Allah will please you with His honor, and it was said: with intercession.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verse 131–132:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾ has two interpretations. The first: he meant by extending the eyes, looking (al-nazar).

The second: he meant by it regret (al-asaf).

﴿Pairs﴾, that is, kinds, derived from al-muzawajah (pairing).

﴿The splendor of the life of this world﴾. Qatadah said: the adornment of the life of this world.

﴿That We may test them thereby﴾, meaning by what We have provided them of this splendor. It has two interpretations. The first: "that We may test them", that is, that We may punish them thereby; this was said by Ibn Bahr.

The second: that We may turn them away from their own interests, and this is a possibility.

﴿But the provision of your Lord is better and more lasting﴾. It has two interpretations. The first: it is contentment with what one possesses and abstention from what one does not possess.

The second: and the reward of your Lord in the Hereafter is better and more lasting than what We have provided these people with in this world.

It may also bear a third meaning: that lawful provision which endures is better than abundance which makes one transgress.

The occasion of its revelation is what Abu Rafi' narrated: "The Prophet ﷺ borrowed food from a Jew, and he refused to lend it except against a pledge. So he grieved and said: (Indeed I am trustworthy in the heaven and trustworthy on the earth; I would carry my armour to him)." Then this verse was revealed.

(p-434) And he narrated that: "When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded his herald, and he called out: Whoever has not been disciplined by the discipline of Allah, the Exalted, his soul will be cut off over the world in regrets."

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And enjoin your family to prayer﴾. It has two interpretations. The first: he meant his family who were fitting for him.

The second: he meant all who followed him and believed in him, because by obedience to him they take the place of his family.

﴿And be steadfast in it﴾, that is, be patient in performing it and in commanding them to it.

And ﴿We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you﴾. Although this is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, what is meant is all creation: that He, the Exalted, provides for them and does not seek provision from them, and benefits them and does not benefit from them. This was more emphatic in bestowing favor upon them.

﴿And the best outcome is for the God-fearing﴾, that is, a good outcome belongs to the people of taqwa (God-consciousness).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 20, verses 133–135:

﴿Say: "Each one is waiting."﴾ That is, each one is awaiting (muntazir). It may bear two meanings. The first: each is awaiting victory over his companion.

The second: the manifestation of the truth in his deed.

﴿So wait;﴾ and this is a threat.

﴿So you will come to know who are the companions of the even path (al-sirat al-sawiyy) and who has been guided.﴾ It may bear two meanings. The first: you will come to know, through victory, who is more rightly guided to the religion of truth.

The second: you will come to know on the Day of Resurrection who is more rightly guided to the path of Paradise, and Allah knows best.
